scenes.title: Recover the original offer
scenes.narration: Start with the original customer, task, promise and scope. Reference the assumption comparison. Keep source status honest. If evidence is absent, say the change is a proposed hypothesis, not a proven improvement.

scenes.title: Choose a focus
scenes.narration: Choose a specific customer and task context to explore. Explain why it fits the learning question and what is outside scope. Narrowing a focus is a learning choice; it does not prove that other customers lack the problem.

scenes.title: Change one priority element
scenes.visual: Keep / Clarify / Narrow / Revise / Pause cards
scenes.narration: Keep a bounded offer, clarify wording, narrow the context, revise the proposed benefit or pause unresolved work. Choose one priority change where possible so the next check is interpretable. More features do not automatically resolve weak evidence.

scenes.title: Write an honest revised offer
scenes.narration: Label the revision and preserve the original. Explain what changed and why. Disclose prototype/manual limits and unproven benefits. Do not add unsupported speed, savings, payment or demand claims to make the offer sound stronger.

scenes.title: Review trade-offs and retest
scenes.narration: Record what the refinement excludes and which assumptions changed. Consider contradictory sources and alternatives. A revised offer needs a new appropriate check; old evidence does not automatically validate new wording, features or audiences.

scenes.title: Build the refinement brief
scenes.narration: Create your Offer Refinement Brief with original version, evidence basis, focus, priority change, revised offer, trade-offs and retest plan. The prototype changes no live product and approves no launch.

sections.label: 02 / LEARN
sections.heading: Refine a proposal without rewriting the evidence.

children: Focus
defines the customer/task context you choose to explore. A
refinement
is a deliberate change to wording, audience, proposed benefit or scope. A
retest
checks the assumptions affected by that change.
Preserve the original offer/version and its assumptions.
Review evidence fit and source status from Lesson 36.
Choose one customer/task focus and explicit exclusions.
Select a priority change: keep, clarify, narrow, revise or pause.
Write a labeled revised proposal, with capability and benefit limits.
Record trade-offs, changed assumptions and a next permitted check.
Evidence-led change
When actual relevant sources challenge wording or scope, explain that connection and retain its limits. Do not generalise a narrow finding to every audience.
Evidence still unknown
A refinement can be a proposed learning hypothesis. Label it as such, keep customer claims unknown and plan a check; do not fabricate justification.
Illustrative proposed refinement

V1: “An event tool for everyone.” V2: “A proposed clear registration entry point for first-time adult visitors in this event context.” Change: narrow audience/task and clarify wording. Evidence: planned/rehearsal only; not a proven improvement. Exclusions: no payment, loyalty or full event operations. Retest: an appropriately permitted uncoached explanation check; access pending.

Old evidence about one audience or prototype does not automatically validate a revised audience, feature or promise. Adding many features can make it harder to tell which change mattered. Preserve contradictory information and alternative refinements; include what you give up.

Do not add untested speed, savings or revenue numbers. Use anonymous planning notes only here. Earlier drafts are reviewed manually; no product update, evidence verification or live offer publication is connected.
